title: Emotional Intelligence · Episode 2
chapters: Anger: why letting off steam backfires
Shame and guilt: the self-conscious emotions
Grief: what really happens when we lose someone

units.t: Emotional Intelligence. Episode two.
In this episode: Anger: why letting off steam backfires, Shame and guilt: the self-conscious emotions and Grief: what really happens when we lose someone.
Part one. Anger: why letting off steam backfires.
Punch a pillow, scream into the void, smash plates in a rage room.
It feels like it should help.
The research says it usually makes things worse.
What anger is for.
Anger has a bad reputation, but it exists for a reason.
It flares when we feel wronged, blocked or treated unfairly, and it prepares the body to push back.
Heart rate and blood pressure rise, adrenaline surges, muscles tense and attention narrows onto the problem.
In our evolutionary past that energy helped people defend food, territory or family.
Today it can still be useful.
Anger signals that something matters, it can give us courage to stand up for ourselves or others, and it has fuelled many campaigns against injustice.
The trouble is not feeling anger.
It is what we do next, and one of the most popular answers is wrong.
The steam engine theory.
Aristotle wrote about catharsis, the purging of emotions, when he described how audiences felt after watching tragedy.
Centuries later Sigmund Freud and others pictured emotions as fluid or steam in a closed system.
Bottle it up and the pressure grows until it bursts out somewhere harmful.
Let it out safely and you return to calm.
This hydraulic picture shaped twentieth century advice: hit a punching bag, scream into a pillow, play violent games to get aggression out of your system.
It lives on in rage rooms, where customers pay to smash crockery and old televisions.
The picture feels right because anger feels like pressure.
But feelings are not steam, and the brain is not a kettle.
The punching bag test.
In 2002 psychologist Brad Bushman tested catharsis on about 600 university students.
Each wrote an essay and received harsh feedback, supposedly from another student, including that it was one of the worst essays the reader had seen.
One group then hit a punching bag while thinking about the person who insulted them.
A second hit the bag while thinking about getting fit.
A third sat quietly for a couple of minutes.
Afterwards everyone could blast their insulter with unpleasant noise through headphones.
The group who vented while focused on their anger felt the most anger and were the most aggressive.
The quiet group were the least angry and least aggressive.
Doing nothing beat letting off steam.
Why venting feeds anger.
Venting fails because it is rehearsal.
Replaying an insult, ranting about it or acting out hitting someone keeps the alarm system switched on and the offence at the front of your mind.
Psychologists call the mental version rumination, one of the strongest predictors of anger lasting longer and spilling onto innocent targets.
A revved-up body is also primed to read new frustrations as further attacks.
In 2021 Sophie Kjærvik and Brad Bushman pooled more than 150 studies.
Activities that lower arousal, such as slow breathing, relaxation, mindfulness, yoga and simply pausing, reliably reduced anger.
Hitting things, and in some studies vigorous exercise straight after a provocation, generally did not.
Regular exercise still helps mood.
When you are boiling, though, cool the body first: breathe out longer than you breathe in, step away, or delay your reply.
Using anger well.
Stuffing anger down has costs too, including strain on relationships and health.
The skill lies between exploding and bottling.
Once the first surge settles, ask what the anger points to.
Was a boundary crossed?
Is something unfair?
Then say so plainly, focusing on the behaviour and its effect rather than attacking the person.
'I was embarrassed when the mistake was raised in front of everyone' invites a conversation.
'You always humiliate me' invites a fight.
Talking helps only when it moves towards understanding or solving the problem.
Anger that is understood can lead to useful change.
Anger that is merely released usually leads to more anger.
If anger often arrives too fast and hard, harms relationships, or has been linked to violence, see a GP for a referral.
In immediate danger, call 000.
The key idea: Anger is an emotion built to confront perceived wrongs, and the trouble lies in what we do with it.
Part two. Shame and guilt: the self-conscious emotions.
They both make your face burn, but shame and guilt pull you in opposite directions.
One tends to help you repair; the other tends to make you hide.
Learning the difference can change how you treat yourself and others.
Two kinds of sting.
Imagine you forget a close friend's birthday.
One inner voice says, 'I did a thoughtless thing, I should call and make it up to her.'
Another says, 'I'm a terrible friend, I always let people down.'
Both are painful, but they are different emotions.
Psychologist June Tangney and her colleagues, who have studied this for decades, put it neatly: guilt is about a bad thing I did, while shame is about being a bad self.
The behaviour is the same, but the focus differs.
Guilt targets a specific action that can be changed.
Shame targets the whole person, which feels far harder to fix.
That small shift in focus has big consequences for what people do next.
Self-conscious emotions.
Fear and joy appear early, but shame, guilt, embarrassment and pride emerge later, typically in the toddler years, once children see themselves as separate people who can be evaluated.
These self-conscious emotions involve imagining how you look to others.
They likely helped our ancestors live in groups, nudging people to follow shared rules, repair damage and avoid rejection.
Darwin was fascinated by blushing, which he saw as a uniquely human expression.
In 1946 anthropologist Ruth Benedict contrasted 'shame cultures' with 'guilt cultures'.
Later scholars found this too neat, and she wrote without visiting Japan.
People everywhere feel both emotions, though cultures differ in triggers and expression.
No society runs on only one.
Repair or hide.
People prone to guilt rather than shame are more likely to apologise, accept responsibility and put things right.
Guilt says the problem is the action, so the solution is a better action.
Tangney's research links guilt-proneness with empathy.
Excessive guilt over things that were not your fault is exhausting, but healthy guilt works like a moral compass.
Shame says the problem is you, and since you cannot swap yourself out, the instinct is to escape.
People avoid eye contact, stop answering messages or hide the mistake.
Shame-proneness is also linked with defensiveness and anger: 'It's not my fault, it's yours.'
That is why shaming people often backfires.
Brené Brown argues that shame thrives on secrecy and silence, and loses some grip when spoken about.
Online pile-ons.
Public shaming is ancient.
Communities once used stocks, pillories and public notices to humiliate wrongdoers.
Social media has revived the practice at enormous scale.

A clumsy joke or an angry moment caught on camera can be shared millions of times within hours, and the target may face abuse, lose a job and find their name permanently linked to the worst moment of their life.
Writer Jon Ronson explored such cases in his 2015 book So You've Been Publicly Shamed.
Accountability for genuine harm matters, but crowds rarely calibrate the punishment to the offence, and the shame-anger cycle can make people dig in rather than reflect.
Before joining a pile-on, ask whether you are aiming for repair, or just enjoying the feeling of righteousness.
Turning shame around.
The split between shame and guilt is partly about how we talk to ourselves, and that can be practised.
When you catch yourself thinking 'I'm an idiot', try 'I made a mistake, and here's what I can do about it.'
Research on self-compassion suggests that responding to failure with kindness, rather than harsh self-attack, makes people more likely to take responsibility and improve, not less.
Talking to a trusted person also helps, because shame shrinks when shared and met with understanding.
This is general information, not therapy.

If shame feels constant or overwhelming, a GP or psychologist can help, healthdirect lists mental health services across Australia, and Lifeline, 13 11 14, is there any time if you are struggling to cope or feel unsafe.
The key idea: Guilt focuses on what you did, while shame focuses on who you are.
Part three. Grief: what really happens when we lose someone.
The famous five stages of grief were never meant to be a map.
Here is what researchers have learned about how people actually carry loss, and why there is no single right way to do it.
Not a staircase.
In 1969 the Swiss-American psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross published On Death and Dying, describing denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.
She had been listening to people who were terminally ill, not to people who had lost someone.
Over time the stages escaped the book and became a checklist, and grieving people sometimes worried they were doing it wrong because they skipped anger or circled back to denial.
Later research has not found that people move through fixed stages in a set order.
Kübler-Ross herself later said the stages were never meant to tidy messy emotions into neat packages.
They can still be useful words for feelings that turn up, but grief is less a staircase than weather: changeable, overlapping and different for everyone.
Grief lives in the body.
People who are grieving often describe it physically: a heavy chest, a hollow stomach, exhaustion that sleep does not fix.
Many cannot concentrate, lose things or reread the same page again and again, a fog sometimes called grief brain.
Appetite can vanish or swing the other way.
These reactions make sense, because losing someone close is a major stress and the body's stress systems respond.
In rare cases, a sudden emotional shock is linked to a temporary heart condition called takotsubo cardiomyopathy, nicknamed broken heart syndrome, where part of the heart muscle suddenly weakens.
Most people recover.
The broader point is that grief is not weakness.
It is a whole-body response to a real and painful change in your world.
Swinging between two worlds.
Picture a widower who spends a morning crying over old photos, then an afternoon learning to cook his wife's meals, then an evening watching football and briefly forgetting.
Dutch researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described this in their dual process model.
One side is loss-oriented: remembering, yearning, feeling the pain.
The other is restoration-oriented: handling practical tasks and taking breaks from sorrow.
People cope best moving between the two.
Laughing at a funeral is not a betrayal.
Psychologist George Bonanno found that the most common pattern after bereavement was not long collapse but real sadness with fairly stable functioning.
People can absorb more loss than we assume, and there is no need to force one kind of grief.
Keeping the bond.
For much of the twentieth century, the advice was to let go: detach from the dead and reinvest your feelings elsewhere.
In 1996 a book called Continuing Bonds, edited by Dennis Klass, Phyllis Silverman and Steven Nickman, challenged that idea.
It argued that many mourners keep an ongoing relationship with the person who died, and that this is often comforting.
Think of someone who talks to a late parent at the cemetery, wears a grandmother's ring, cooks a family recipe on an anniversary, or asks what a lost friend would say about a decision.
Across many cultures, rituals honour ancestors and keep their memory alive.
The goal of grieving is not to forget.
It is to find a new place for the person in a life that continues.
Hidden and prolonged grief.
Not every loss comes with a funeral or sympathy cards.

Researcher Kenneth Doka coined the term disenfranchised grief for losses that are not openly acknowledged, such as a miscarriage, the death of an ex-partner, a pet, or a parent slowly lost to dementia.
Naming the loss helps, as does a small ritual like planting a tree.
Simply saying 'I know this matters, and I'm sorry' can mean more than advice.
For most people the sharpest pain softens over months and years.
For a minority, intense yearning and an inability to re-engage with life persist; this is now recognised as prolonged grief disorder, and effective therapies exist.
This is general information, not medical advice.
Talk to your GP, see healthdirect, or call Lifeline on 13 11 14 if you are struggling.
The key idea: The five stages of grief began as observations of dying patients, not a rulebook for mourners.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is the main problem with anger according to this lesson?
Answer. What we do with it, because the feeling can be useful.
Question two. According to June Tangney's framing, what is the core difference between guilt and shame?
Answer. Guilt is about the act; shame is about the self.
Question three. What is the best way to view the five stages of grief?
Answer. As useful words for feelings, not a fixed order.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
